questions.text: Have you written down who is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity, and shared those roles across your business?
questions.why: Addresses a lack of clear cybersecurity accountability, investment, or effectiveness, which leaves security gaps that no one owns or fixes.
questions.fix: Document cybersecurity roles and responsibilities in a written policy, and name the person accountable for the program.

questions.text: Do you have written cybersecurity policies that leadership reviews and updates at least once a year?
questions.why: Addresses insufficient policies to manage risk; without policies that keep pace with new threats and technology, cyber risk goes unmanaged.
questions.fix: Write down your cybersecurity risk strategy and policies, then schedule a leadership review at least once a year.

questions.text: Do you have a written plan for how you would respond to a cyberattack, and do you practice it at least once a year?
questions.why: Addresses the inability to quickly isolate, contain, eradicate, and communicate about incidents, which lets damage grow unchecked.
questions.fix: Write a basic incident response plan covering your likely scenarios, then run a tabletop drill at least once a year.

questions.text: Do your contracts require vendors and service providers to promptly tell you about security incidents and vulnerabilities in their products?
questions.why: Addresses weak supply chain risk management; a vendor breach or flaw can reach your systems before you ever hear about it.
questions.fix: Add clauses to vendor contracts and service-level agreements requiring notice of security incidents and vulnerabilities within a set timeframe.

questions.text: If an outside company remotely manages your IT or systems, do you track and manage the security risks that relationship creates?
questions.why: Addresses adversaries exploiting trusted third-party access; a compromised managed service provider can hand attackers deep access to your environment.
questions.fix: List the managed service providers with access to your systems, and review their contracts for security duties and incident notification.

questions.text: Do you keep an up-to-date inventory of your organization's hardware, software, data, and systems?
questions.why: Addresses attackers using unknown or unmanaged devices as entry points; you cannot protect assets you do not know you have.
questions.fix: Start a simple inventory of all hardware and software, and update it on a regular schedule, especially for business-critical systems.

questions.text: Do you patch or otherwise fix known security vulnerabilities on your systems in a timely way, especially internet-facing ones?
questions.why: Addresses adversaries who routinely target unpatched, internet-exposed systems, using known software flaws to gain their initial foothold.
questions.fix: Set up a vulnerability management routine, and start by patching anything listed on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog.

questions.text: Do you have an independent expert test whether your security controls actually work, for example through penetration tests?
questions.why: Addresses gaps in cyber defenses or overconfidence in existing protections that have never been tested by an outside party.
questions.fix: Engage a qualified third party to run a penetration test or security assessment, then fix the high-priority findings.

questions.text: Do you give security researchers an easy, public way to report vulnerabilities they find in your systems?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, if researchers cannot easily report weaknesses, flaws stay open longer and adversaries may exploit them first.
questions.fix: Publish a simple way to report vulnerabilities (an email address or web form), and consider a security.txt file per RFC 9116.

questions.text: Do you keep an accurate, up-to-date diagram of how your networks are connected?
questions.why: Addresses an incomplete or inaccurate understanding of network topology, which slows down incident response and recovery.
questions.fix: Create a current network diagram of your IT and any OT networks, and update it whenever the network changes.

questions.text: Do you change the default manufacturer passwords on all new hardware, software, and devices before connecting them?
questions.why: Addresses attackers who look up and reuse default account passwords to gain initial access or move through a network.
questions.fix: Adopt a policy that requires changing every default password before a device or system is connected to your network.

questions.text: Do you require passwords to be long (about 16 characters or more) on the systems that can support it?
questions.why: Addresses adversaries who crack short passwords quickly with brute-force tools, whether online or against stolen password hashes.
questions.fix: Set a system-enforced minimum password length, and encourage passphrases and a password manager to make long passwords easy.

questions.text: Do you make sure accounts use unique passwords, instead of the same password being reused across systems?
questions.why: Addresses reused credentials, which let an attacker who steals one password move laterally across many systems, including between IT and OT.
questions.fix: Give each account and service its own unique password, and use a password manager to keep track of them.

links.label: Have I Been Pwned (check exposed passwords)

questions.text: When someone leaves your organization, do you disable their accounts and collect their badges and keys the same day?
questions.why: Addresses adversaries who abuse the still-active accounts of former staff to get in and avoid detection.
questions.fix: Create an offboarding checklist that revokes all accounts and returns physical access on an employee's departure day.

questions.text: Do you log failed login attempts and get alerted when there is a suspicious burst of them?
questions.why: Addresses automated, credential-based attacks such as password guessing, spraying, and stuffing, which show up as repeated failed logins.
questions.fix: Turn on logging of failed logins, and set an alert for an unusual number of attempts in a short window.

questions.text: Do you require a second factor (like an app or security key) beyond a password to access your important accounts?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, with only a password, an adversary who guesses or steals it can log in freely; MFA adds a second barrier.
questions.fix: Turn on MFA for remote access and privileged accounts first, using phishing-resistant methods (like FIDO security keys) where possible.

questions.text: Do your administrators use a separate account for everyday tasks like email and web browsing, apart from their admin account?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, if an admin's everyday account is compromised, attackers gain administrator access unless privileges are kept separate.
questions.fix: Give administrators a second, standard account for routine work, and reserve admin accounts for admin tasks only.

questions.text: Do you limit each user, role, and process to only the access it actually needs to do its job?
questions.why: Addresses excess access, which lets adversaries move undetected across systems and reach sensitive data and critical systems.
questions.fix: Review access permissions (ideally each quarter), and remove any rights that are not needed for the person's role.

questions.text: Have you divided your network into segments so a breach in one area cannot easily spread to everything else?
questions.why: Addresses a flat network, which lets an intruder who gets in reach sensitive data, spaces, and critical infrastructure unimpeded.
questions.fix: Place routers or firewalls between network zones to separate traffic, and physically segment OT areas where possible.

questions.text: Do all staff get cybersecurity awareness training when they start and at least once a year after that?
questions.why: Addresses untrained users, who are easier targets for phishing, social engineering, and other attacks that rely on human error.
questions.fix: Provide new hires initial security training, run refreshers for everyone at least annually, and add role-based training for key staff.

questions.text: Do you encrypt sensitive data both when it is stored and when it travels across your network?
questions.why: Addresses adversaries positioned on the network who sniff, alter, or steal sensitive and operational data that is not encrypted.
questions.fix: Identify your most sensitive data, apply up-to-date encryption for it in transit and at rest, and never store passwords in plaintext.

questions.text: Have you turned on email security protections like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to fight spoofing and phishing?
questions.why: Addresses attackers who spoof your domain and send convincing phishing emails to your people and customers when these protections are missing.
questions.fix: Enable STARTTLS, SPF, and DKIM on your email, and set DMARC to a reject policy.

questions.text: Do you block Office macros and USB autorun by default, allowing them only when specifically needed?
questions.why: Addresses attackers who rely on users opening files with malicious macros, or on autorun, to execute code on a system.
questions.fix: Set a policy that disables macros and autorun by default, with an approval process for the rare cases that truly need them.

questions.text: Do you have a process to review, test, and approve changes to your systems before they go live?
questions.why: Addresses unmanaged changes, which can break critical systems and make it harder to maintain, respond to, and recover operations.
questions.fix: Put a change management policy in place that requires approval and testing before configuration or system changes are deployed.

questions.text: Do you regularly back up critical systems, store the backups offline, and test that you can actually restore from them?
questions.why: Addresses ransomware and other adversaries that destroy data and disable recovery, so untested or online-only backups may fail when needed.
questions.fix: Back up business-critical systems on a schedule, keep copies offline, and test a full restore at least once a year.

questions.text: Do you require review and approval before new hardware, firmware, or software is installed on your systems?
questions.why: Addresses unapproved or tampered hardware and software, which can introduce compromised products or hidden malware into your environment.
questions.fix: Create an approval process, and keep a list of allowed hardware, firmware, and software with approved versions.

questions.text: Do you collect security logs from your systems and store them securely in a central place?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, without collected and protected logs, you cannot detect intrusions or investigate what an attacker did.
questions.fix: Send security logs to a central system that only authorized staff can access, and alert when a critical log source stops.

questions.text: Do you prevent unauthorized USB drives and other removable devices from connecting to your systems?
questions.why: Addresses attackers who copy malware onto removable media (like USB drives) to breach systems, including disconnected or air-gapped ones.
questions.fix: Set policies that block unauthorized USB and removable media, for example by limiting USB use or disabling ports.

questions.text: Do you make sure internet-facing systems expose no unnecessary services and are kept patched?
questions.why: Addresses adversaries who exploit weaknesses, bugs, or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems to gain their first network foothold.
questions.fix: Keep internet-facing assets patched, remove unneeded services, and never expose management interfaces to the public internet.

questions.text: Do you run antivirus or anti-malware that is kept updated and set to scan automatically on your systems?
questions.why: Addresses malware such as payloads, droppers, and backdoors, which let adversaries control machines, evade defenses, and act after a breach.
questions.fix: Deploy antivirus or anti-malware on your endpoints, keep it updated, and set it to scan email and removable media automatically.

questions.text: Do you have defined criteria and a process to recognize a suspicious security event and escalate it?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, without a way to spot adverse events, initial access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement go unnoticed.
questions.fix: Define what counts as a suspicious event, document how to escalate it, and connect it to your incident response plan.

questions.text: Do you have a plan for who to communicate with, and how, during a cybersecurity incident?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, without set communication procedures, an incident disrupts coordination among responders, slowing resolution and worsening damage.
questions.fix: Write a communications plan that lists internal and external stakeholders and how you will reach them during an incident.

questions.text: Do you have written procedures for who to report a confirmed cyber incident to, and how, including CISA?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, without timely reporting, CISA and others cannot help you or see whether a broader campaign is hitting your sector.
questions.fix: Document to whom and how you report confirmed incidents (regulators, ISACs, CISA), and the timeframes that apply.

questions.text: Can you recover and restore your critical systems after a cyber incident, and do you learn from each one?
questions.why: Addresses the risk that, without recovery plans, a cyber incident can leave critical assets, services, or systems down for a long time.
questions.fix: Build and maintain recovery plans for your critical systems, then run a post-incident review to improve them after any event.
